edges.effect_quant: In the largest meta-analysis of apparently healthy adults, higher versus lower muscular strength was associated with a hazard ratio of 0.69 for all-cause mortality; the dose-response review spanning 3,135,473 participants found an inverse near-linear mortality gradient across common handgrip strength ranges.
edges.population: older adults or aging populations in community-based and prospective cohort studies
edges.mechanism: Low grip strength likely reflects low physiologic reserve more than one isolated pathology. It clusters with sarcopenia, frailty, inflammatory burden, disability, lower cardiorespiratory fitness, and reduced resilience to hospitalization or acute illness, which makes it a useful late-life mortality marker.
edges.summary: This is less a surprising causal discovery than a durable geriatric prognostic signal. Across very large cohorts, older adults with lower grip strength die at higher rates, and the relationship survives adjustment often enough that it is hard to dismiss as mere noise.
edges.caveats: Grip strength is partly a marker of underlying illness rather than a pure intervention target, so the edge should not be read as proof that squeezing exercises alone will reduce mortality. Thresholds also vary by sex, body size, and measurement protocol.

evidence.citation: Garcia-Hermoso A 2018 Arch Phys Med Rehabil
